About: Ideal Gas Lab

Source

Model
A real molecular-dynamics simulation. Constants: heavy particles 28 AMU / 125 pm, light 4 AMU / 87.5 pm, k = 8316 AMU·pm²/ps²·K (the Boltzmann constant in these units; the exact conversion is 8314.46), container 5,000–15,000 × 8,750 × 4,000 pm, injection at 300 K, 0–200 particles per species.
Concept
A container of particles with a pump, a heater, and a movable wall. Macroscopic gauges sit next to the microscopic motion.
Serves
The ideal gas equation and the named slices: Boyle, Gay-Lussac, Charles (Hold Constant).
Inquiry
What happens to the pressure when you add particles? When you squeeze the box?
Misconception
That pressure is a substance stored in the gas — rather than something the motion of the particles produces.

Pedagogy principles applied

IDPrincipleHow it shows up here
H1Misconception is structural, not a text card"The pressure stays the same — it's a property of the gas" is a wrong prediction choice; the wall-bombardment rebuttal appears only if the student picks it.
D6/D7Guided inquiry reveals in stagesFive cards run predict (N) → observe → predict (Boyle) → observe (Gay-Lussac) → resolve (Charles via Hold-Pressure); each stage stages the gas through onStep.
A2Fewest objectsOne container, one pump, one heater. The gauges, width indicator and units are views, not extra apparatus.
CEvery number earns its placeT is computed from the particles' true kinetic energy and P from NkT/V every frame; the readouts are measurements of the simulation, not scripts.
§11Physics honestyParticles undergo genuine elastic collisions (momentum and energy conserved pair by pair); heating rescales real velocities; resizing the container confines the particles without changing their speeds (an isothermal resize — the Hold Constant modes close the thermodynamic loop). Nothing is animated that the physics does not produce — except the optional "Pressure noise" gauge wobble (±0.6%, display-only, toggleable in the View panel).

Guided Inquiry

1 · Predict: pump in more gas

The container holds 50 heavy particles at 300 K in a fixed volume, reading about 590 kPa. If you pump it up to 100 particles (same temperature, same volume), what does the pressure gauge do?

2 · Watch the drumbeat

The particles are already in motion — slide Heavy particles from 50 up to 100 and back. The gauge tracks N in exact proportion — PV = NkT with T and V pinned. Each particle you add is injected at 300 K through the pump port and joins the bombardment within moments.

3 · Predict: squeeze it

Now in Laws mode with temperature held constant: 100 particles at 300 K. You will halve the volume (10,000 → 5,000 pm). What happens to the pressure?

4 · Heat at fixed volume

Volume is now held constant. Push the Heat slider up and hold it: the flame pours energy into the particles, the thermometer climbs, and the gauge climbs in lock-step — P ∝ T (Gay-Lussac). Cool it and both fall together. Faster particles hit harder and more often.

5 · The container breathes

Finale: Pressure is held constant (↕V). Heat the gas and watch the container expand on its own — the wall retreats exactly enough to keep the drumbeat steady: V ∝ T (Charles's law). One equation, PV = NkT, ties every knob together. Hit Finish and explore both modes freely — and mind the lid at high pressure…

01

At a glance

A box of gas has a movable left wall, a pump on the right and a burner underneath. A thermometer and a pressure gauge sit above the box, and four readouts keep the count.

What you'll learn

  • What the gauge pressure and the thermometer temperature measure in a box of moving particles.
  • How the particle count, the temperature and the volume are linked to the pressure.
  • How to read the Hold constant setting to run one gas law at a time.
A box of gas with a wall you can move, a pump and a burner.

What's on screen

  • The box: heavy particles in purple and light ones in orange, bouncing off the walls and each other.
  • Thermometer: sits above the box and reads the temperature in kelvin.
  • Pressure gauge: a dial on the right, with the pressure printed underneath.
  • Readouts (sidebar): T, P, the particle count N and the container width.
See itOpen the sim with its opening gas: 50 heavy particles and nothing held. Watch for: 300 K on the thermometer, 50 particles, and a container width of 10,000 pm.

On the canvas, drag the left wall to change the width between 5,000 and 15,000 pm. Drag the pump handle down to inject particles. The temperature stays between 50 and 1000 K, and the lid blows off above 20,000 kPa.

03

Pressure comes from wall hits, so it grows with the particle count

Every particle that bounces off a wall gives it a tiny push. The pressure is the total push on each unit of wall area. More particles in the same box mean more hits each second, and so a larger pressure.

P = N k T / V
N is the number of particles, k the Boltzmann constant, T the temperature and V the volume.

At 300 K in the 10,000 pm box, 50 particles read about 592 kPa. Doubling to 100 gives about 1,184 kPa, and 200 gives about 2,367 kPa. The pressure is proportional to N when T and V stay fixed.

The pump does the same job. Dragging its handle down injects particles, and the Pressure readout steps up with every one added.

See itSet 100 heavy particles in the same box at 300 K. Watch for: Pressure at about 1,184 kPa, twice the 592 kPa of 50 particles, while T stays 300 K.
04

Temperature is the average kinetic energy, so light particles move faster

The thermometer reads T from the motion of the particles themselves. Each particle carries an average kinetic energy of 3kT/2, whatever its mass.

½ m vrms2 = 3kT / 2
vrms is the root-mean-square speed of the particles.

At the same T, a lighter particle must move faster. The light particles here have 4 AMU and the heavy ones 28 AMU, so vrms differs by √(28/4) = √7 ≈ 2.65. At 300 K that is about 517 m/s for heavy particles and 1,368 m/s for light ones.

The pressure formula has no mass in it. Swap 50 heavy particles for 50 light ones at the same T and V, and the wall still takes the same number of pushes of the same total size.

See itFill the box with 50 heavy and 50 light particles at 300 K. Watch for: 50 + 50 = 100 in the N readout, Pressure at about 1,184 kPa, the same as 100 heavy, and the orange particles moving faster.
05

Squeezing the gas raises the pressure, and P × V stays constant

Hold the temperature fixed and move the wall. A narrower box gives the particles less room, so they reach each wall more often and the pressure rises. This is Boyle's law.

P V = constant (N and T fixed)
Halve the volume and the pressure doubles.

The box has a fixed height and depth, so its volume is proportional to its width. With 100 particles at 300 K:

WidthPressureP × width
15,000 pm789 kPa11.8 × 106
10,000 pm1,184 kPa11.8 × 106
7,500 pm1,578 kPa11.8 × 106
5,000 pm2,367 kPa11.8 × 106
See itChoose Laws mode, hold the temperature, and close the wall from 10,000 to 5,000 pm. Watch for: the Width readout falling to 5,000 pm, T staying at 300 K, and Pressure rising from 1,184 to about 2,367 kPa.
06

Heating at fixed volume raises the pressure in proportion to T

Hold the volume and heat the gas. The particles move faster, so each one hits the wall harder and more often. This is Gay-Lussac's law.

P / T = N k / V = constant (N and V fixed)
Double the kelvin temperature and the pressure doubles.

The temperature must be in kelvin, because P is proportional to T measured from absolute zero. For 100 particles in the 10,000 pm box, P / T = 1,184 / 300 ≈ 3.95 kPa/K. At 450 K the pressure is about 1,775 kPa, and at 600 K it is about 2,367 kPa.

The Heat / Cool slider springs back when you release it, so the gas keeps the temperature it reached.

See itChoose Laws mode, hold the volume, and heat the gas for a few seconds. Watch for: T and Pressure climbing together from 300 K and 1,184 kPa, with the Width readout staying at 10,000 pm.
07

Heating at fixed pressure expands the gas in proportion to T

Now let the wall move freely and hold the pressure. When the gas is heated, the harder hits push the wall outward until the hits per unit area fall back to the same pressure. This is Charles's law.

V / T = N k / P = constant (N and P fixed)
Double the kelvin temperature and the volume doubles.

Start 100 particles at 6,000 pm and 300 K, where the pressure is about 1,973 kPa. The width then follows the temperature at 6,000 / 300 = 20 pm per kelvin: 9,000 pm at 450 K and 12,000 pm at 600 K.

The wall stops at 15,000 pm, which this gas reaches at 750 K.

See itStart at 6,000 pm, hold the pressure with the wall, and heat the gas for a few seconds. Watch for: T rising from 300 K while the Width readout grows past 6,000 pm, and Pressure staying near 1,970 kPa.
08

Where it matters

  • Combining the laws. The three laws are one equation, PV = NkT. In exam problems, use it with T in kelvin and write the ratio form P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ when N is fixed.
  • Tyre pressure. A tyre warms as you drive, and its volume barely changes. The pressure rises in proportion to the kelvin temperature, which is why the gauge reads higher on a hot road.
  • Sealed cans. A closed container heated by a fire has a fixed volume. P / T stays constant, so the pressure can climb until the lid or wall gives way, just as the lid blows off in the sim above 20,000 kPa.
Go deeper: why N k T and not the mass

Each wall hit changes a particle's momentum by 2mv, and the hits per second go as v/L. The pressure then goes as N m v² / V, and since m v² is proportional to kT, the mass drops out. This is why 50 light and 50 heavy particles give the same pressure at the same T. Real gas molecules also move in three dimensions, while this sim draws a flat box.

09

Summary

In one line. This sim is a box of bouncing particles whose pressure comes from wall hits, so you can see how the count, the temperature and the volume set it.

Key points

  • The ideal gas law is PV = NkT. At 300 K and 10,000 pm, 100 particles read about 1,184 kPa.
  • Boyle: at fixed T, P V is constant. Gay-Lussac: at fixed V, P / T = 3.95 kPa/K. Charles: at fixed P, V / T = 20 pm/K from 6,000 pm.
  • T is the average kinetic energy, and the pressure does not depend on the particle mass.

Common mix-ups

  • "Light particles make less pressure because they weigh less." They move faster, and 50 light particles give the same pressure as 50 heavy ones at the same T and V.
  • "Doubling the Celsius temperature doubles the pressure." Use kelvin. From 300 K to 600 K the pressure doubles, but from 30 °C to 60 °C it rises by only about 10%.
  • "Heating at fixed volume changes the number of particles." N is unchanged. Each particle hits harder and more often.

Things to try on your own

  • Predict the pressure for 150 heavy particles at 300 K, then set the sliders and compare.
  • Hold the pressure and cool the gas to 150 K. Predict the width first.
  • Use the pump to double the count while holding the volume and the temperature.
